paras.text: Contracts, HIFA, Risk and Warranty — Michigan Residential Builder Exam Lecture

Welcome back. This chapter covers the Contracts slice of the Business and Law section. On the PSI exam, that's about seven questions out of the fifty Business and Law questions. The territory is contract fundamentals, the Home Improvement Finance Act, the Home Solicitation Sales Act, the written contract rule in the Construction Lien Act, statutes of limitations, and warranties. This is one of the most trap-heavy areas of the whole exam, because Michigan has four different statutes that each do something different, and wrong answers are built by attributing one statute's rule to another. So let's untangle them once and for all.
Start with the map. Four laws, four different jobs.

Law number one: M C L five seventy point eleven fourteen, part of the Construction Lien Act. This is the written contract rule that actually matters for builders. It says a contractor has no construction lien on a residential structure unless the work was done under a written contract, and — listen carefully — any amendments or additions to that contract are also in writing. The contract must also contain a statement that residential builders, electricians, plumbers, and mechanical contractors are required to be licensed, and if your work requires a license, the contract must say you are licensed and must include your license number. There is no dollar threshold. Any amount. A five hundred dollar handyman job and a two hundred thousand dollar addition are treated the same. No written contract with the license number, no lien. And a verbal change order means the added scope has no lien protection either.

Law number two: M C L three thirty nine point twenty four twelve, in the Occupational Code. An unlicensed builder cannot sue to collect compensation for residential work. Period. You can do the work, you just can't use the courts to get paid.

Law number three: M C L three thirty nine point twenty four oh three. This is where the famous six hundred dollar number lives. Work where labor and materials combined come to under six hundred dollars is exempt from the licensure requirement. Hear me clearly: that is a licensure exemption, and only a licensure exemption. It is not a written contract trigger. If an exam answer says contracts over six hundred dollars must be in writing under HIFA, that answer is wrong twice over.

Law number four is HIFA itself, the Home Improvement Finance Act, Act three thirty two of nineteen sixty five, M C L four forty five point eleven oh one and following. HIFA is a financing statute. It applies only when the homeowner pays on credit through the contractor — an installment contract or a charge agreement — and only when the cash price is more than three hundred dollars. Exactly three hundred dollars is not covered; it has to exceed three hundred. New home construction is completely excluded. Commercial property is excluded. A loan the homeowner gets directly from their own bank is excluded. Free standing appliances like a stove or refrigerator are excluded. And one more time for the people in the back: there is no section four forty five point eleven oh eight. It does not exist. Never pick an answer built on it.

Now, when HIFA does apply, it is picky about the paperwork. The contract must be dated and in writing, with the printed portion in at least eight point type. The words home improvement installment contract must appear in at least ten point bold, either at the top or right above the buyer's signature. There's a required notice to the buyer in bold type with four messages: don't sign before you read; you're entitled to a completely filled in copy; you can pay off early and get a partial refund of the finance charge; and you can rescind the contract.

The contract also has to itemize the money. Cash price. Down payment. Unpaid cash balance. Insurance premiums if any. Official fees. Principal amount financed. The finance charge, in dollars. The time balance, the number and amount of installments, and the time sale price. If one installment is a balloon — substantially bigger than the others — the contract needs a bold legend saying this contract is not payable in installments of equal amounts, with the amount and due date spelled out.

Here's a favorite exam fact: the contractor must hand the buyer a completed copy of the contract at the time it's signed. Until that completed copy is delivered, the buyer is not obligated to pay. That's section twelve oh four.

HIFA also has its own rescission right, and this is a huge trap, so slow down with me. Under HIFA, the buyer may rescind the contract until five P M on the business day following the date of the contract. One business day, ending at five in the afternoon. That is not the three day right you've heard about. The three day right comes from a different law — the Home Solicitation Sales Act — and it runs to midnight of the third business day. Two different statutes, two different clocks. HIFA: five P M, next business day. Home solicitation: midnight, third business day. If a question mixes a door to door sale with contractor financing, the buyer gets both rights.

HIFA bans certain contract provisions outright, under section twelve oh six. You cannot make the buyer waive claims or defenses, against you or against a finance company that buys the paper. You cannot give the holder the power to accelerate the balance arbitrarily when the buyer isn't in default. You cannot make the buyer waive the right to sue over illegal collection tactics. You cannot authorize breaking into the property or breaching the peace to repossess. And here's the one that surprises builders: you cannot put a liquidated damages clause in a HIFA contract that pays you for the buyer's cancellation or rescission. In ordinary construction contracts, a reasonable liquidated damages clause — say, per day delay damages — is enforceable if it's a genuine pre-estimate of harm and not a penalty. But in a HIFA installment contract, liquidated damages for cancellation are flat out prohibited. The offending clause is void, though the rest of the contract survives. On top of that, section fourteen oh nine says no act, agreement, or statement of the buyer is a valid waiver of any protection under the act. The buyer literally cannot sign away HIFA rights.

What happens if you willfully violate HIFA? It's a misdemeanor. Up to ninety days in jail, a fine up to five hundred dollars, or both, for a first offense. Repeat offenses go up to a year. And paying someone a reward or referral fee to procure a home improvement finance contract is also prohibited.

Now the Home Solicitation Sales Act, Act two twenty seven of nineteen seventy one, M C L four forty five point one eleven through one seventeen. This applies to seller solicited sales at the buyer's home — the classic storm chaser at the kitchen table. The buyer can cancel until midnight of the third business day after signing. A mailed cancellation counts when it's dropped in the mailbox, properly addressed with postage paid — not when you receive it. The contract must have the cancellation statement right next to the signature line, plus a notice of cancellation form in duplicate. And the seller cannot send a courier to grab the buyer's payment at the house before the three days run out.

There is an emergency exception, and the exam loves it. To cut off the buyer's cancellation right in an emergency, three things must all be true. First, the buyer asked for the goods or services without delay because of an emergency. Second, the seller in good faith made a substantial beginning of performance before any cancellation notice. And third — this is the one to memorize — the buyer gave the seller a separate, dated, signed personal statement, in the buyer's own handwriting, describing the emergency and expressly waiving the three day right. Handwriting. Not typed, not a checkbox on your form. That handwritten statement is a Michigan statutory requirement, and the federal cooling off rule requires it too. For restoration work — a burst pipe, a tree through the roof — get that handwritten waiver before you set a single fan, or you're working at your own risk.

If the buyer does cancel in time, you must return every payment, any trade-in, and any signed note within ten business days of receiving the notice. Business days, not calendar days. The buyer makes any delivered goods available at the house, and if you don't pick them up within twenty days, the buyer keeps them free.

Let's shift to contract fundamentals, because PSI tests the national material too. A valid contract needs five elements: offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, and legality. Consideration means each side gives something of value. If a party lacks capacity — a minor, for instance — the contract is voidable by that party. An illegal contract is simply void.

Know your contract types by who eats the cost risk. Fixed price, also called lump sum: the contractor bears the risk. Overrun the budget, you eat it; beat the budget, you keep the savings. Cost plus: the owner bears the risk, paying actual costs plus your fee. Time and materials: the owner again, paying hourly labor and materials, usually where scope is uncertain. Unit price: shared — you carry the unit cost risk, the owner carries the quantity risk.

Change orders: written, signed by both parties, describing the scope change and the price or time adjustment. In Michigan that's not just best practice — remember, written amendments are a lien rights condition.

Substantial completion means the owner can use the work for its intended purpose. It triggers release of retainage — typically five to ten percent held from progress payments — and starts the warranty clock. Final completion means every punch list item is done. On breach: a material breach excuses the other party's performance; remedies include compensatory damages, rescission, quantum meruit for the value of work performed, and rarely specific performance. And the injured party always has a duty to mitigate — you can't run up damages you could reasonably have avoided.

Now the clocks — the statutes of limitations. Breach of contract in Michigan: six years, under M C L six hundred point fifty eight oh seven, subsection nine. Negligence causing injury to a person or property: three years, under M C L six hundred point fifty eight oh five, subsection two. And then the big one, the statute of repose, M C L six hundred point fifty eight thirty nine. For claims arising from a defective or unsafe improvement to real property — against a contractor, architect, or engineer — the action must be brought within six years from occupancy, use, or acceptance of the completed improvement. Not from discovery. From occupancy. A defect discovered in year seven is simply barred, even though nobody could have found it earlier. The only exception is gross negligence: then the claimant gets one year after the defect is discovered or should have been discovered, but never more than ten years after occupancy. So the ten year number is only the cap on the gross negligence exception — it is not the general rule. Limitations versus repose in one breath: limitations runs from the breach or injury; repose runs from a fixed event and kills the claim regardless of discovery.

Warranties come in three layers. Express warranties are written promises in the contract — enforceable exactly as written. The implied warranty of habitability says a new home sold by a builder vendor must be fit for human habitation — Michigan recognizes it, but Michigan courts may enforce a disclaimer, so it is not untouchable. The implied warranty of workmanship says the work must meet the standard of a reasonably skilled tradesperson, and it exists whether or not the contract mentions it. Classic scenario: bad flashing leaks three years in, and the one year express warranty has expired. The homeowner's best theory is the implied warranty of workmanship — still alive, still within the six year windows.

Round it out with insurance. Commercial general liability covers third party bodily injury, third party property damage, and personal and advertising injury — never your own work product or your own property. Builder's risk covers the structure while it's being built, plus materials on site and in transit, and it ends at occupancy. Errors and omissions covers design mistakes, which C G L excludes. Umbrella coverage adds limits and may broaden coverage; excess only adds limits. A certificate of insurance is a snapshot — it proves coverage existed on the day it was issued, nothing more. An additional insured endorsement puts the general contractor on the sub's policy. A waiver of subrogation stops an insurer from chasing the named party after paying a claim. And the liability theories: negligence needs duty, breach, causation, and damages; strict liability applies to defective products with no fault needed; vicarious liability means the general contractor can answer for a sub's actions on the site.

Rapid fire recap. Say these out loud with me. HIFA trigger: cash price over three hundred dollars, on installment credit, existing homes only. HIFA rescission: five P M, next business day. HIFA type sizes: eight point body, ten point bold headings. HIFA copy rule: no completed copy, no duty to pay. HIFA penalty: misdemeanor, ninety days, five hundred dollars. Liquidated damages for cancellation in a HIFA contract: prohibited and void. Home solicitation cancellation: midnight of the third business day. Emergency waiver: separate, dated, signed, in the buyer's own handwriting. Refund after cancellation: ten business days. Goods pickup: twenty days or the buyer keeps them. Licensure exemption: under six hundred dollars, labor plus materials. Unlicensed builder: cannot sue to collect. Lien rights: written contract, license number, written change orders, any dollar amount. Contract statute of limitations: six years. Negligence: three years. Statute of repose: six years from occupancy, use, or acceptance. Gross negligence: one extra year after discovery, capped at ten. Retainage: five to ten percent, released at substantial completion. Five contract elements: offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, legality. Four negligence elements: duty, breach, causation, damages.
If you can rattle those off cold, you own all seven contracts questions. Next chapter, we move on. Keep driving.
